messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir is a 34-year-old publisher who lives with his wife, Nadia, in a midsized American city. Fifteen months ago, he and Nadia were riding a downtown bus when a man boarded, pulled a knife, and attacked Nadia without warning. Amir tried to shield her but was thrown to the floor; he lay there, pinned, listening to her scream and watching blood spread across her coat. The image of the knife blade, the sound of her voice breaking, the helplessness of his own body—these came at him in disjointed fragments that never quite formed a complete story. For weeks afterward he would hear those screams in his head, sometimes so vividly that he checked the room for an intruder.

The bus became impossible. The first time Amir tried to ride it again, his heart hammered before he even reached the stop: he studied every passenger's face, noting the way a man held his bag, the shape of a woman's keys in her hand. That scanning for threat was automatic now, and exhausting. He came to believe that if he could just see danger coming early enough, he might stop it—but the effort drained him completely. By the end of a single ride he would be trembling and so tired that his thoughts felt sticky, and in that exhausted state the memory of the attack would rush back, the film of Nadia's face and the knife playing over and over until he could not tell whether he was remembering or reliving. The tiredness itself became a trigger: when he stayed late at the office, or when insomnia took hold, his guard dropped and the disorienting pieces would surface.

At work, Amir managed a team of editors. He now avoided going anywhere unfamiliar—lunch spots, client meetings across town—because he could not assess the danger. He had even begun to note potential weapons everywhere: a letter opener on a desk, a scissors in a supply closet, a long-handled umbrella. That vigilance looped back on itself. When he scanned a colleague's face and saw nothing but normalcy, he felt a sharp relief, but the scanning itself would summon the bus, the knife, the scream. And the harder he searched for safety, the more unsafe everything felt. Vulnerability pressed in at odd moments: showering, changing clothes, being naked—the exposure made him want to cover his skin, and that physical feeling of nakedness would unlock the memory of lying helpless on the bus floor. He began to dread the evenings when he was too tired to keep his mind occupied, because then the auditory flashbacks came sharper, the disconnected pieces pressing in.

The cumulative weight of these cycles reshaped his marriage. Nadia survived her physical injuries, but Amir could not bring himself to ride the bus with her again; he insisted on driving, and even then he circled blocks to avoid particular streets. He became irritable when she wanted to try a new restaurant. She did not understand why he studied the faces of their dinner companions, or why he flinched when a server approached with a tray that could, in his mind, become a weapon. Amir knew he was pushing her away, but he could not stop searching for the threat he was certain was coming.

What finally brought him to seek help was a single moment last month: exhausted after a sleepless night, he sat on his living room couch, and for ten minutes he could not remember whether the attack on Nadia had actually happened or whether he was trapped inside one of the replaying images. The world felt unreal, and he was terrified that he was losing his mind. He came to the clinic hoping someone could make the film stop—but what frightened him most was the thought that if he stopped scanning, stopped avoiding, the next attack would happen and he would fail her again.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that the memory leads to or causes the experience of triggers; instead triggers lead to memory.
